newsitem.title: USA: NYS budget to have hospital, tuition plans--papers.
newsitem.headline: NYS budget to have hospital, tuition plans--papers.

text.p: New York State's budget likely will restore deep Medicaid cuts that Governor George Pataki initially proposed and help parents save for their childrens' college education, published reports said Tuesday.

Newsday said the new budget was expected to include two top priorities of hospitals, nursing homes and healthcare companies -- the elimination of Pataki's planned Medicaid cuts, which totaled $800 million, and a five-year phase-out of the so-called "sick tax," which eventually will save the healthcare industry $550 million a year.
The paper cited state and industry officials.

Pataki has made reining in the state's $24 billion Medicaid program a top priority. But healthcare providers said the cuts would hurt their ability to care for poor and needy patients, as well as other individuals, whose bills help subsidize indigent care, the paper said.
It added that the new fiscal 1998 budget was not expected to try to restore about $700 million that Pataki cut from the program in the 1997 budget.

New York State's budget was due on April 1, and legislators, according to some reports, were expected to begin drafting approving passages as soon as Thursday, though Newsday said the Senate Majority Leader said that would be impossible as no budget was agreed to by late Monday.

The Daily News, in its Tuesday edition, said that the new budget would include tuition payment programs that would let parents and grandparents invest up to $5,000 a year for public or private college without paying state income taxes. The paper cited sources close to the talks. When the funds invested were withdrawn, the childrens' tax rate would apply.

The paper added that the Democrat Assembly Speaker said the savings plan would not allow a child to go to the State University of New York or the City University of New York based on the present tuition rates, as the Republican-led Senate had proposed.

In its Tuesday edition, the New York Times said disputes over welfare were blocking lawmakers from approving a new budget, including a fight between Pataki and Assembly Democrats, who want workfare participants to be paid the minimum or, if higher, the prevailing wage.
Pataki, who does not want either wage scale to apply and who was supported by New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, also wants to keep workfare costs down by not letting participants join unions.
However, the new budget pact preliminarily agreed to by Congress would require workfare participants to be paid the minimum wage.

The paper added that Assembly Democrats had dropped their insistence that a budget pact close a loophole in the state's new rent rules that allows landlords to raise rates for vacant apartments by more than 20 percent. Instead, the Democrats hold out hope that the Republican Pataki Administration administratively do away with the bigger increase.
